title: Domestic abuse, FGM and safeguarding
blurb: Ask about domestic abuse safely, respond to disclosure, apply the FGM reporting duty correctly and share information under the 2026 duty.
question: Hodan, 26, is at her booking appointment. Type 3 FGM is noted on examination, and she has a 3-year-old daughter at home. Her husband insists on staying and interpreting. What should the midwife do?

teach.h: Two people to protect, often more
teach.body: A midwife safeguards the woman, her unborn baby and any other children in the home. Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 (which replaced the 2023 edition) is the statutory guidance in England; some parts of it apply to unborn children through early pre-birth assessment, and its glossary defines physical abuse, emotional abuse, sexual abuse and neglect. Neglect may occur during pregnancy as a result of maternal substance abuse. An abusive partner may also try to stop a woman attending her appointments (NICE CG110).

teach.caption: NICE NG201 1.2.5 and CG110 1.1.14: every woman should have at least one consultation without her partner or family present.

head: Action
Detail
rows: Confidential record, NOT the hand-held notes
Consider a domestic abuse support worker
Named midwife for most of her care
Professional interpreter, never partner or family

teach.h: FGM: is the mandatory report required?

children.edge: Girl under 18 tells you or you see signs
children.label: Report to police yourself
children.sub: Call 101 within one month (FGM Act s5B)

children.label: No mandatory report
children.sub: Safeguarding risk assessment for daughters and unborn girl

teach.caption: The s5B duty cannot be passed to a safeguarding lead to make for you.

teach.body: Since 30 September 2026, s16LA of the Children Act 2004 requires relevant agencies, including NHS bodies, to share information relevant to a child's safeguarding or welfare with other such agencies. No threshold must be met first, consent is not required, and sharing does not breach confidence. The exception is where sharing would be more harmful to the child than not sharing. Practitioners should normally still be open with the family about what they share, unless that would put the child at risk.
teach.cite: Children Act 2004 s16LA (CWSA 2026); Information sharing duty guidance, Sept 2026

teach.body: The midwife politely explains that every woman is seen alone for part of booking and arranges a professional interpreter, not her husband. Alone, she asks about domestic abuse and about Hodan's FGM in a kind, sensitive way (NG201 1.2.6). Hodan is an adult, so there is no mandatory police report, but her daughter, and her baby if a girl, may be at risk, so a safeguarding risk assessment and referral follow local procedures. Everything is recorded in the confidential record.

teach.text: The FGM police duty is for GIRLS UNDER 18 who tell you or whose signs you see. An adult's FGM does not trigger s5B, but it does trigger a safeguarding look at her daughters. And the old 'seven golden rules' of information sharing are no longer current: the s16LA duty replaced that approach for children.

items: Ask about domestic abuse at booking or the earliest chance when she is alone; use professional interpreters.
Record disclosures confidentially, not in hand-held notes; give helpline information; consider a specialist support worker.
Children who see, hear or experience domestic abuse are victims in their own right (Domestic Abuse Act 2021 s3).
FGM s5B: girl under 18 tells you or you see signs, report personally to police within one month.
Adult FGM: safeguarding assessment for daughters and unborn girls; no mandatory police report.
s16LA (from 30 Sep 2026): share safeguarding information about children; consent not required.

summary: You can now carry out routine enquiry about domestic abuse safely and respond to disclosure, decide when the FGM mandatory reporting duty applies and what to do for adult women, and share information about children under the 2026 statutory duty. You can also recognise when an unborn baby needs pre-birth safeguarding.

A.q: According to NICE NG201, when should a midwife ask a pregnant woman about domestic abuse?
options: At booking, with her partner present for support
At booking or the earliest chance when she is alone
At 28 weeks, once rapport has been built
At booking, using a relative to interpret
A.why: NG201 1.2.5: ask about domestic abuse in a kind, sensitive manner at booking, or at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, with a chance for private one-to-one discussion.

whyNot.0: A partner may be the abuser; enquiry must happen when she is alone.
whyNot.2: Enquiry should start at booking, not be delayed to 28 weeks.
whyNot.3: Relatives must not interpret; a professional interpreter is needed (CG110 1.3.10).

A.q: Amira, 16, tells the midwife at booking that she had FGM as a young child. What must the midwife do?
options: Ask the safeguarding lead to report it for her
Refer to children's social care instead of police
Report it to the police herself within one month
Record it, as reporting does not apply in pregnancy
A.why: FGM Act 2003 s5B: a regulated professional told by a girl under 18 that she has had FGM must personally notify the police within one month.

whyNot.0: The duty is personal and cannot be passed to a safeguarding lead.
whyNot.1: The mandatory duty is to the police; safeguarding referral is in addition, not a substitute.
whyNot.3: Pregnancy does not change the duty; she is under 18.

A.q: Bella discloses domestic abuse at her 16-week appointment. Where should the midwife record this?
options: In a confidential record, not the hand-held notes
In the hand-held notes so every clinician sees it
In a letter to the GP that Bella carries
On the summary sheet she shows her partner
A.why: NICE CG110 1.5.8: tell the woman the information will be kept in a confidential record and not in her hand-held record, which her abuser may read.

whyNot.1: Hand-held notes may be seen by the abuser and put her at risk.
whyNot.2: A letter she carries could be read by the abuser.
whyNot.3: Anything her partner sees could put her in danger.

B.q: Hodan, 26, has type 3 FGM noted at booking. She has a 3-year-old daughter. Which action is required?
options: Report Hodan's FGM to the police within one month
Assess the safeguarding risk to her daughter and unborn baby
Ask Hodan's husband to confirm the history
Take no further action, as Hodan is an adult
B.why: For a woman aged 18 or over, the s5B police duty does not apply, but a safeguarding risk assessment for her daughter and unborn girl is needed.

whyNot.0: s5B covers girls under 18; Hodan is an adult.
whyNot.2: Her husband should not be used to confirm a confidential history.
whyNot.3: Adult FGM still raises safeguarding questions for her daughter.

B.q: Shirin tells the midwife her partner hit her in front of her 4-year-old son last week. She begs the midwife not to tell anyone. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Respect her wishes, as sharing needs consent
Wait to see whether it happens again first
Share with children's social care and tell her why
Share it after a second incident is reported
B.why: Her son is a victim of domestic abuse (Domestic Abuse Act 2021 s3). Under s16LA (from 30 Sept 2026) information relevant to his safeguarding must be shared; consent is not required, but she should normally be told.

whyNot.0: Consent is not required for sharing under the s16LA duty.
whyNot.1: Waiting leaves the child at risk; there is no threshold to wait for.
whyNot.3: No threshold or second incident is needed before sharing.

B.q: Which statement about children and domestic abuse is correct under the Domestic Abuse Act 2021?
options: Children count as victims if they are physically hurt
Children under 5 are too young to be affected
Children are witnesses in law, not victims
A child who sees or hears the abuse is a victim
B.why: Domestic Abuse Act 2021 s3: a child who sees, hears or experiences the effects of abuse, and is related to either party, is a victim in their own right.

whyNot.0: Seeing, hearing or experiencing the effects is enough; physical injury is not required.
whyNot.1: Babies and young children are affected and are recognised as victims.
whyNot.2: The Act recognises children as victims, not witnesses.

C.q: Mira, 20 weeks, attends with her husband, who answers every question and says he will interpret. Mira seems withdrawn. What is the best next step?
options: Let him interpret and ask about abuse later
Book a professional interpreter and see her alone
Ask him to leave and use their daughter to interpret
Ask gently about abuse with him in the room
C.why: NG201 1.2.5 and CG110 1.3.10, 1.1.14: use an independent interpreter, not a partner or family member, and make sure she has time alone to discuss sensitive issues.

whyNot.0: Using him as interpreter prevents safe disclosure at every visit.
whyNot.2: Family members, including children, must not interpret.
whyNot.3: Asking in front of a possible abuser can put her at greater risk.

C.q: On a postnatal visit, Fatou, 25, says her 12-year-old sister had FGM abroad last summer. The midwife has not seen the girl. What applies?
options: Report to police under s5B within a month
Make a safeguarding referral under local procedures
Record it, as the girl is not her patient
Ask Fatou to bring her sister for examination
C.why: The s5B duty applies when the girl herself discloses or signs are seen. A disclosure by a sibling or parent needs a normal safeguarding referral.

whyNot.0: s5B is not triggered by a third-party disclosure.
whyNot.2: Any professional who learns a child may be at risk must act, patient or not.
whyNot.3: Arranging an examination is not the midwife's role; refer to the safeguarding system.

C.q: Leah is 30 weeks pregnant, using heroin daily and has missed most appointments. Her two older children are in care. What is the most appropriate safeguarding action?
options: Wait until the birth, as the fetus is not covered
Discharge her from care for non-attendance
Tell her the baby will be removed at birth
Refer to children's social care for pre-birth assessment
C.why: Working Together 2026 applies parts of its guidance to unborn children through pre-birth assessment; neglect can begin in pregnancy through maternal substance use.

whyNot.0: Pre-birth assessment exists for exactly this situation.
whyNot.1: Non-attendance is a warning sign that needs more contact, not discharge.
whyNot.2: Outcomes are decided through assessment; a midwife must not pre-empt them.

reteach.title: Alone, under 18, share
reteach.question: Three words can steer most safeguarding questions in pregnancy. What are they?

blocks.body: ALONE: ask about domestic abuse when she is on her own, with a professional interpreter. UNDER 18: the FGM police report is for girls under 18 who tell you or whose signs you see; adults trigger a safeguarding look at their daughters. SHARE: since 30 September 2026, information about a child's safety is shared without needing consent.

blocks.text: A partner or relative must not interpret, however helpful they seem. A professional interpreter protects disclosure.

explain.body: Ask every woman about domestic abuse at booking or the earliest chance she is alone, kindly and privately, and give opportunities to talk at every visit (NG201 1.2.5, 1.2.10).

test.q: Which interpreter should be used for routine enquiry about domestic abuse?
options: Her partner, who speaks English
Her mother, who lives with her
A professional interpreter
Her teenage son, who is fluent
test.why: CG110 1.3.10 and NG201 1.1.11: interpreters should be independent of the woman, not family, friends or partner.

whyNot.0: Her partner may be the abuser.
whyNot.3: Children must not interpret, especially about abuse.

explain.body: Keep a confidential record (not hand-held notes), give a helpline card, consider referral to a domestic abuse support worker, offer a named midwife and flexible appointments (CG110 1.5).

test.q: Why is a domestic abuse disclosure not written in the hand-held notes?
options: They are not legal records
The abuser may read them
GPs cannot access them
They are destroyed after birth
test.why: CG110 1.5.8: a confidential record protects the woman, because her abuser may see the hand-held notes.

whyNot.0: Hand-held notes are part of the legal record.
whyNot.2: Access by GPs is not the reason.
whyNot.3: Hand-held notes are not destroyed after birth.

explain.body: In England and Wales, a regulated professional told by a girl under 18 that she has had FGM, or who sees signs, must personally report to the police (101) within one month (FGM Act 2003 s5B).

test.q: A midwife sees signs of FGM in a 17-year-old. By when must she report to the police?
options: Within 24 hours
Within one week
Within one month
Within three months
test.why: FGM Act 2003 s5B: the report must be made before the end of one month from discovery.

whyNot.0: The legal limit is one month, although sooner is fine.
whyNot.1: The legal limit is one month, not one week.
whyNot.3: Three months exceeds the legal limit.

explain.body: From 30 September 2026, s16LA Children Act 2004 requires agencies including the NHS to share information relevant to a child's safeguarding or welfare. No threshold, consent not required, no breach of confidence; exception if sharing is more harmful to the child.

test.q: Under the s16LA information sharing duty, when may a midwife decide NOT to share safeguarding information about a child?
options: When the parent refuses consent
When sharing would harm the child more
When the concern is below threshold
When she fears a complaint
test.why: s16LA: the exception is where disclosure would be more detrimental to the child than not disclosing.

whyNot.0: Consent is not required under the duty.
whyNot.2: No threshold has to be met before sharing.
whyNot.3: Fear of a complaint is not the statutory exception; s16LA(3) allows only greater harm to the child.
